state.misconception_label: Has used slant height and base to find area of a triangle rather than perpendicular height and base

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: How would you calculate the area of this triangle? ![A triangle, base 12m. All three sides are equal.](). I got \( \frac{12 \times 12}{2} \) because I added the side lengths instead of multiplying.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Why do you think adding the side lengths gives you the area of the triangle? Can you explain why using the slant height and base might not be the best approach in this case?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, I think I was confused... I used 12 twice because I thought the side of the triangle was the same as the height? But now I'm not sure - is the slant height different from the actual height we're supposed to use for the area formula?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you think of a different way to determine the height of the triangle that aligns with the formula for calculating its area? How might using the slant height instead of the perpendicular height affect the accuracy of your calculation?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the slant vs. perpendicular height misconception through questioning, the student shows clear progress in understanding the distinction, though the teacher could have provided slightly more concrete guidance on how to find the perpendicular height.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's thinking, never provides direct answers, and helps expose the flaw in confusing slant height with perpendicular height through questioning.
